newsitem.title: UK: Information sharing needs sensible handling - LME.
newsitem.headline: Information sharing needs sensible handling - LME.

text.p: Exchange of information between global futures exchanges and industry regulators is evolving all the time, although the issue needs careful handling, London Metal Exchange (LME) Chief Executive David King said.

The LME was one of the first markets to sign up to the U.S. Futures Industry Association (FIA) task force set up in March 1995 after the Barings Bank debacle, resulting in the Exchange sharing information with 48 other exchanges.
"But information sharing has to be sensibly handled," King said in an interview.

"We have never knowingly purposefully withheld information, while being very conscious of the confidentiality issue and the legal constraints imposed on us by the Financial Services Act (FSA) and European legislation," he said.
These prohibit the LME passing on certain types of information, he said.

The need for co-operation between the world's futures exchanges and regulators was highlighted by the collapse of Barings Bank in early 1995 after unauthorised trading in Singapore by its head trader there, Nick Leeson.

"One of the reasons we had great interest (in information sharing) was that was a prime example of a financial debacle which touched many markets, basically Europe, South America and South East Asia," King said.

Since then and closer to home the LME has been directly affected by the huge losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading by Sumitomo Corp's former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka, although the Japanese firm is not an LME member.
King said that information sharing will not stand still, and there will be further changes.

"We see this as being an evolutionary process...It will be driven by technological advances which force the regulatory authorities around the world to adopt a global regulatory communications network," he said.
One area that stands out is the explosive growth of the Internet, where people can trade, can solicit business, and transfer money.
"There are a whole new raft of potential issues which are already being addressed," King said.
Another development from the Sumitomo affair is the wholesale review of the LME being carried out by Britain's top regulator the Securities and Investments Board (SIB).

"The LME is supportive of the SIB review process, which is taking place at the invitation of the LME...But it is premature to make any announcements as to the potential outcome of the review," King said.
The SIB report is scheduled to report by the end of the year. It recently issued a consultative document, which all members of the metals industry are urged to respond to.
King declined to comment on whether he anticipated radical changes in procedures. But "the LME has never been afraid to change, and we are in a constant state of evolution," he said.
He was hopeful that the fall-out from the Sumitomo affair would not have a long lasting impact on the LME.

"We are optimistic that market activity will continue to be healthy through 1997, and we will continue to strive to make the LME a safe place in which to carry out base metals hedging business," he added.
